<reason>Side A won by maintaining a consistent framework that public service requires universal, controlled infrastructure rather than rented platform distribution. They effectively turned Side B's "doorway" concession into evidence that prioritizing short-form hollows out the core service. A's rebuttals were sharper and more decisive, particularly the distinction between staff journalists and external creators with opposing loyalties. Side B's opening was clipped (execution cost) and their later rounds, while competent, were more defensive and repetitive, failing to neutralize A's core argument that prioritizing ephemeral platform presence sacrifices durable public value.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 1 turning Side B's "doorway" metaphor into an attack on the prioritization logic, arguing that funding the entrance over the building "hollows out the destination" and treats essential channels as sunk costs.</best_rebuttal>
